newsitem.title: USA: Calif water supply seen recovering from early thaw.
newsitem.headline: Calif water supply seen recovering from early thaw.

text.p: Although recent heavy rainfall eroded much of northern California's lower elevation snowpack, water supplies have a good chance of recovering to above-average levels, industry sources said Tuesday.
"If this thing continues, this will go down as a very wet year," James Bailey, spokesman for the Califoria Department of Water Resources (DWR).
"With a wet year following another wet year, we are going to be lousy with water."
An analyst at the National Weather Service in Sacramento said "We've still got a good portion of winter snow accumulation to go."
He noted recent storms erased much of the snowpack below 6,500 feet (2,000 meters), but snow above that elevation was largely untouched.
As of January 6, statewide snowpack totaled 140 percent of the average seasonal level, according to the weather center.
DWR has indicated that deliveries to state water utilities will be limited to 75 percent of contract amounts for the current water year (October 1, 1996-September 30, 1997).
But spokesman Bailey said those projections are typically "very conservative" and likely to rise as the water year progresses.
He added, "The big probelm now is we've got so much water they are going to be dumping water for the next month or two."
Bailey noted a portion of snowpack was melted by the heavy rain and "it could happen that this very wet year could turn around and we would have dryness."
But groundwater tables in the mountains remain high, indicating reservoirs will refill regardless of new precipitation, he said.
"We had good carryover (in the reservoirs) from last year," Bailey explained. "Water saturation is high. Depending on the geology of individual projects, this contributes to healthy river flows."
